entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 6 Is 6:1-13 . Vision of Jehovah in His Temple. Isaiah is outside, near the altar in front of the temple. The doors are supposed to open, and the veil hiding the Holy of Holies to be withdrawn, unfolding to his view a vision of God represented as an Eastern monarch, attended by seraphim as His ministers of state ( 1Ki 22:19 ), and with a robe and flowing train (a badge of dignity in the East), which filled the temple. This assertion that he had seen God was, according to tradition (not sanctioned by Is 1:1 ; see Introduction), the pretext for sawing him asunder in Manasseh's reign ( He 11:37 ). Visions often occur in the other prophets: in Isaiah there is only this one, and it is marked by characteristic clearness and simplicity. 1. In ... year ... Uzziah died-- Either literal death, or civil when he ceased as a leper to exercise his functions as king [Chaldee], (2Ch 26:19-21). 754 B.C. [Calmet] 758 (Common Chronology). This is not the first beginning of Isaiah's prophecies, but his inauguration to a higher degree of the prophetic office: Is 6:9 , &c., implies the tone of one who had already experience of the people's obstinacy. Lord-- here Adonai, Jehovah in Is 6:5 ; Jesus Christ is meant as speaking in Is 6:10 , according to Joh 12:41 . Isaiah could only have "seen" the Son, not the divine essence ( Joh 1:18 ). The words in Is 6:10 are attributed by Paul ( Ac 28:25 , 26 ) to the Holy Ghost. Thus the Trinity in unity is implied; as also by the thrice "Holy" ( Is 6:3 ). Isaiah mentions the robes, temple, and seraphim, but not the form of God Himself. Whatever it was, it was different from the usual Shekinah: that was on the mercy seat, this on a throne; that a cloud and fire, of this no form is specified: over that were the cherubim, over this the seraphim; that had no clothing, this had a flowing robe and train.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8419"/><div sID="gen13545" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8419"/><hi type="bold">2. stood--</hi>not necessarily the posture of standing; rather, were in attendance on Him [Maurer], hovering on expanded wings.<div eID="gen13545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the--</hi>not in the Hebrew.<div eID="gen13546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seraphim--</hi>nowhere else applied to God's attendant angels; but to the fiery flying (not winged, but rapidly moving) serpents, which bit the Israelites (<reference osisRef="Num.21.6">Nu 21:6</reference>), called so from the poisonous inflammation caused by their bites. Seraph is to burn; implying the burning zeal, dazzling brightness (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.11">2Ki 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.17">6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.13">Eze 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.3">Mt 28:3</reference>) and serpent-like rapidity of the seraphim in God's service. Perhaps Satan's form as a serpent (nachash) in his appearance to man has some connection with his original form as a seraph of light. The head of the serpent was the symbol of wisdom in Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Num.21.8">Nu 21:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.4">2Ki 18:4</reference>). The seraphim, with six wings and one face, can hardly be identified with the cherubim, which had four wings (in the temple only two) and four faces (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.5-Ezek.1.12">Eze 1:5-12</reference>). (But compare <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Re 4:8</reference>). The "face" and "feet" imply a human form; something of a serpentine form (perhaps a basilisk's head, as in the temples of Thebes) may have been mixed with it: so the cherub was compounded of various animal forms. However, seraph may come from a root meaning "princely," applied in <reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Da 10:13</reference> to Michael [Maurer]; just as cherub comes from a root (changing m into b), meaning "noble."<div eID="gen13547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">twain--</hi>Two wings alone of the six were kept ready for instant flight in God's service; two veiled their faces as unworthy to look on the holy God, or pry into His secret counsels which they fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.6">Ex 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.15">15:15</reference>); two covered their feet, or rather the whole of the lower parts of their persons--a practice usual in the presence of Eastern monarchs, in token of reverence (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.11">Eze 1:11</reference>, their bodies). Man's service a fortiori consists in reverent waiting on, still more than in active service for, God. <div eID="gen13548" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 8. I ... us-- The change of number indicates the Trinity (compare Ge 1:26 ; 11:7 ). Though not a sure argument for the doctrine, for the plural may indicate merely majesty, it accords with that truth proved elsewhere. Light enough is given in revelation to guide those sincerely seeking to know, in order that they may do, God's will; darkness enough is left to confound the wilfully blind (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.8">Is 43:8</reference>). So in Jesus' use of parables ( Mt 13:14 ). see ... indeed-- rather, "though ye see again and again," yet, &c.
entries.reader_content_plain: 9. Hear ... indeed-- Hebrew, "In hearing hear," that is, Though ye hear the prophet's warnings again and again, ye are doomed, because of your perverse will ( Joh 7:17 ), not to understand. Light enough is given in revelation to guide those sincerely seeking to know, in order that they may do, God's will; darkness enough is left to confound the wilfully blind ( Is 43:8 ). So in Jesus' use of parables ( Mt 13:14 ). see ... indeed-- rather, "though ye see again and again," yet, &c.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8427"/><div sID="gen13569" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8427"/><hi type="bold">10. Make ... fat--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.119.17">Psa 119:17</reference>). "Render them the more hardened by thy warnings" [Maurer]. This effect is the fruit, not of the truth in itself, but of the corrupt state of their hearts, to which God here judicially gives them over (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.17">Is 63:17</reference>). Gesenius takes the imperatives as futures. "Proclaim truths, the result of which proclamation will be their becoming the more hardened" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Ro 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>); but this does not so well as the former set forth God as designedly giving up sinners to judicial hardening (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.8">Ro 11:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11">2Th 2:11</reference>). In the first member of the sentence, the order is, the heart, ears, eyes; in the latter, the reverse order, the eyes, ears, heart. It is from the heart that corruption flows into the ears and eyes (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.21">Mr 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.22">22</reference>); but through the eyes and ears healing reaches the heart (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.17">Ro 10:17</reference>), [Bengel]. (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.21">Jr 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.2">Eze 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.7.11">Zec 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.57">Ac 7:57</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.4">2Ti 4:4</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Matt.13.15">Mt 13:15</reference>, the words are quoted in the indicative, "is waxed gross" (so the Septuagint), not the imperative, "make fat"; God's word as to the future is as certain as if it were already fulfilled. To see with one's eyes will not convince a will that is opposed to the truth (compare <reference osisRef="John.11.45">Joh 11:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.11.46">46</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.10">12:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.12.11">11</reference>). "One must love divine things in order to understand them" [Pascal].<div eID="gen13569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be healed--</hi>of their spiritual malady, sin (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Is 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.14">Jr 17:14</reference>). <div eID="gen13570" type="x-p"/>

In English Version, "return" refers to the poor remnant left in the land at the Babylonish captivity (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.14">2Ki 24:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.12">25:12</reference>), which afterwards fled to Egypt in fear (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.26">2Ki 25:26</reference>), and subsequently returned thence along with others who had fled to Moab and Edom (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.11">Jr 40:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.12">12</reference>), and suffered under further divine judgments.<div eID="gen13575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tell--</hi>rather, "terebinth" or "turpentine tree" (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Is 1:29</reference>).<div eID="gen13576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">substance ... when ... cast ... leaves--</hi>rather, "As a terebinth or oak in which, when they are cast down (not 'cast their leaves,' <reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job 14:7</reference>), the trunk or stock remains, so the holy seed (<reference osisRef="Ezra.9.2">Ezr 9:2</reference>) shall be the stock of that land." The seeds of vitality still exist in both the land and the scattered people of Judea, waiting for the returning spring of God's favor (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Ro 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.23-Rom.11.29">23-29</reference>). According to Isaiah, not all Israel, but the elect remnant alone, is destined to salvation. God shows unchangeable severity towards sin, but covenant faithfulness in preserving a remnant, and to it Isaiah bequeaths the prophetic legacy of the second part of his book (the fortieth through sixty-sixth chapters). <chapter eID="Isa.6"/>

navigation_sections.content_plain: CHAPTER 6 Is 6:1-13 . Vision of Jehovah in His Temple. Isaiah is outside, near the altar in front of the temple. The doors are supposed to open, and the veil hiding the Holy of Holies to be withdrawn, unfolding to his view a vision of God represented as an Eastern monarch, attended by seraphim as His ministers of state ( 1Ki 22:19 ), and with a robe and flowing train (a badge of dignity in the East), which filled the temple. This assertion that he had seen God was, according to tradition (not sanctioned by Is 1:1 ; see Introduction), the pretext for sawing him asunder in Manasseh's reign ( He 11:37 ). Visions often occur in the other prophets: in Isaiah there is only this one, and it is marked by characteristic clearness and simplicity.
